headline: ASX closes up 0.37% as PLS surges 2.4% and GOOG hits fresh highs, while Iran-US tensions keep oil elevated and the RBA's next rate call hangs in the balance.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara had a solid session, up 2.4% to $4.64. No single big catalyst today — the move likely reflects a broader lift in materials stocks as commodity sentiment improved. Lithium pricing remains depressed and PLS is still well below its highs, so this is a bounce rather than a trend reversal.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: GOOG climbed 1.9% in last night's session to $357.33 USD. Multiple analysts flagged accelerating Search revenue growth as the driver — the market is rewarding Alphabet's ability to maintain search dominance even as AI competition heats up. GOOG has been a consistent outperformer relative to the broader market lately.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI rose 1.8% today to $16.44, riding positive sentiment around AI stocks broadly. GOOG's strong session overnight and continued AI investment news out of Canberra helped lift the sector. Still down about 13% from cost base, so the long road back continues.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE nudged up 0.41% today. The Aussie dollar's rise (up nearly 1% to ~70 US cents) can actually work against this ETF's AUD-denominated returns when emerging market assets are priced in USD, but broad emerging market sentiment held up reasonably well today.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG was essentially flat today, up just 0.07%. As a diversified fund holding Australian and international shares, it tracks the broader market steadily. The ASX was up modestly and US markets were mixed last night, so a quiet day is about right.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS dipped 0.27% today to $532.81. The AUD rose sharply today (up ~1% vs USD), which weighs on this ETF since it holds US assets — a stronger Aussie dollar reduces the AUD value of those US holdings. No issue with the underlying US market; this is purely a currency effect.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: No fresh price data available for MSFT tonight. The big date to watch is July 29 — that's when Microsoft reports quarterly earnings. Multiple analysts are flagging it as a potential major catalyst, with cloud and AI revenue in the spotlight. Previous close was $390.99 USD.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: No fresh price data for TTWO tonight. News flow is mostly GTA 6 speculation and commentary — nothing fundamental has changed. The stock's long-term thesis is still tied to the GTA 6 release cycle. Previous close was $244.10 USD.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — Bounce continues, but stay patient
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals is up 2.4% today to $4.64, which is encouraging, but it's still down 31% from your cost base. The long-term thesis — that lithium demand will recover as EV adoption grows — remains intact. No reason to sell, and the dip could be a top-up opportunity for patient investors. Hold for now.

watch_today.title: MSFT — Earnings on July 29 are the event to watch
watch_today.detail: Microsoft reports quarterly earnings on July 29 (US time). Analysts are split — some say the stock could 'go parabolic' if Azure cloud and AI Copilot revenues impress; others flag a 'crisis of confidence' that needs repairing. As a long-term holder, you'd want to sit tight through any volatility rather than react. Hold and watch.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — AI sentiment lifting, but still underwater
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF is up 1.8% today, riding good vibes from GOOG's strong session and Canberra's new AI policy push. Still down ~13% from what you paid. The long-term case for AI infrastructure investment is as strong as ever — hold and let the thesis play out.

watch_today.title: RBA rate decision looming — watch your mortgage/cash
watch_today.detail: The Reserve Bank's next rate call is approaching, and The Guardian is reporting a fourth rate rise becomes more likely if the Iran-US conflict isn't resolved within a week. Higher oil prices (up 1.4% today to $80.47 USD) feed into inflation, which gives the RBA less room to cut. If you have a variable-rate mortgage or cash savings, keep this on your radar.

watch_today.title: GOOG — Strong run, long-term hold
watch_today.detail: GOOG is up 1.9% last night to $357.33 USD and is now 16% above your cost base. The driver is accelerating Search revenue growth — the market is rewarding Google for holding its ground against AI competitors. No reason to sell. If anything, this reinforces the long-term hold case.

watch_today.title: Oil up 1.4% on Iran-US tensions — watch inflation flow-on
watch_today.detail: Crude oil hit $80.47 USD a barrel today as Iran claimed it attacked a US base in Jordan. Higher oil means higher petrol prices and broader inflation pressure in Australia, which matters for RBA decisions and consumer stocks. Nothing to act on directly, but it's a risk worth monitoring this week.

world.summary: The US-Iran conflict has escalated sharply, with Iran claiming a major attack on a US base in Jordan. Trump is set to make a major address on elections, China is courting Europe, and Singapore's economy is showing signs of cooling.

stories.title: Iran claims major attack on US base in Jordan as US-Iran conflict escalates
stories.source: ABP Live English / ABC7 New York / PBS
stories.why_it_matters: Iran has claimed responsibility for a major attack on a US military base in Jordan, a significant escalation in an already dangerous conflict. The US had previously struck Iran, and Tehran has now retaliated across the broader Middle East. Middle East experts warn this threatens a return to all-out war. For Australians, the flow-on is real: oil prices are rising (up 1.4% today to $80.47/barrel), which eventually means higher petrol prices and inflation. At least 16 Indian nationals have been killed or gone missing since the conflict began, signalling the human cost is spreading beyond the direct combatants.

stories.title: Trump to give major Thursday address revisiting 2020 election fraud claims
stories.why_it_matters: President Trump has announced he'll deliver a major speech on Thursday focused on 'free and fair elections' — widely interpreted as revisiting his claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. The address is being watched closely as it could inflame domestic political tensions in the US at a time when the country is already managing a military conflict with Iran. Politically, it signals Trump is doubling down on electoral grievances rather than unifying the country, which could add to market uncertainty.

stories.title: China's Wang Yi tours Nordic countries in charm offensive for Europe
stories.why_it_matters: China's top diplomat Wang Yi is on a Nordic tour aimed at strengthening China-Europe ties. The move is widely seen as Beijing trying to drive a wedge between Europe and the US at a time when US-China trade tensions remain elevated. For Australia, stronger China-Europe economic links could shift global trade flows — and China remains Australia's largest trading partner, so Beijing's diplomatic manoeuvrings always matter to our export economy.

stories.title: Singapore's economic growth slows to 5.7% in Q2
stories.why_it_matters: Singapore's economy grew 5.7% in the second quarter of 2026, a slowdown from earlier in the year. Singapore is often seen as a bellwether for Asian trade and economic health given its role as a regional hub. A slowdown there can signal cooling demand across Asia — relevant for Australian exporters who rely heavily on Asian markets, and for holdings like VGE which tracks emerging markets broadly.

stories.title: Middle East conflict squeezes consumers and businesses in New Zealand — and Australia next?
stories.why_it_matters: The Middle East conflict is already hitting New Zealand consumers and businesses through higher fuel and shipping costs. As a close neighbour with a very similar economic structure to Australia, what hits NZ often arrives here shortly after. Businesses are reporting squeezed margins and reduced consumer confidence — a preview of what Australian businesses may face if oil prices stay elevated.

markets.summary: The ASX 200 closed up a modest 0.37% today at 8,841. Oil jumped 1.4% on Iran-US tensions, gold eased slightly, and the Aussie dollar had a strong day rising nearly 1% against the greenback. US markets (S&P 500 and NASDAQ) don't have fresh data yet — they open tonight at 11:30 PM AEST.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Modest gain today, supported by materials and tech stocks.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's close — no change data available. Opens tonight 11:30 PM AEST.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Last night's close — no change data available. Opens tonight 11:30 PM AEST.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Up on Iran-US conflict escalation. Feeds into Australian petrol prices.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Slight pullback despite geopolitical tension — unusual but not alarming.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Strong day for the Aussie, pushing toward 70 US cents. Good for overseas travel and imports, but weighs on AUD value of US stock holdings.

politics.summary: Big day in Australian policy: the Albanese government has launched a major AI framework including new rules for data centres and a crackdown on AI copyright theft. The RBA's next rate call is looming large, and a report on energy affordability shows one in five Aussies can't afford their power bill.

stories.title: Albanese government launches national AI framework — data centres to face power grid mandate
stories.why_it_matters: Prime Minister Albanese has unveiled a national AI framework that forces data centres to connect to the electricity grid in a specific way — essentially making them accountable for the enormous amounts of power they consume. The government is also flagging a crackdown on AI companies using Australian creators' copyrighted content without permission. The policy is aimed at attracting large-scale AI investment to Australia while protecting workers and rights-holders. A separate ABC report notes a 60-year-old foreign investment law could determine whether billions in AI data centre investment actually lands here — the government may need to reform it.

stories.title: RBA rate rise more likely if Iran conflict drags on beyond a week
stories.why_it_matters: The Guardian is reporting that a fourth consecutive RBA interest rate rise becomes significantly more likely if the Iran-US military conflict isn't resolved within the week. Higher oil prices feed into inflation, which gives the Reserve Bank less room to ease — or more reason to keep tightening. Brokers and lenders are placing their bets ahead of the next RBA board meeting. If you're on a variable-rate mortgage, this is the single most important domestic story to follow right now.

stories.title: One in five Australians can't afford their power bill under Albanese government
stories.why_it_matters: A new report shows 20% of Australians — one in five — cannot afford to pay their electricity bill under the current government. Despite the government's energy bill relief payments, high electricity prices remain a major cost-of-living pressure. The finding is politically damaging for Labor ahead of any future election, and underscores why energy policy — including the new data centre grid rules — is so central to Australian politics right now.

stories.title: Hundreds of thousands more students face higher university fees
stories.why_it_matters: Hundreds of thousands of additional Australian students are set to be hit with higher university fees under changes moving through parliament. The story describes the situation as 'not fair at all' — suggesting the fee increases fall on a broad range of students, not just those in premium courses. Higher education costs are a long-running political battleground, and this adds to cost-of-living pressures already squeezing younger Australians.

ai.summary: Australia's government made its biggest AI policy move yet today. Globally, protesters marched on the big AI labs, Meta launched a new developer model, and the debate about how to regulate AI — and whether regulation even asks the right questions — is heating up.

stories.title: Albanese government mandates data centre grid rules and cracks down on AI copyright theft
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government today released a national AI framework with two big practical changes: data centres must connect to the electricity grid under new rules (making them accountable for their massive power use), and the government flagged action against AI companies that scrape and use Australian creators' copyrighted content without permission or payment. This matters to investors because it could affect where big tech companies choose to build AI infrastructure in Australia — and companies like Google and Microsoft are directly impacted.

stories.title: Protesters march on OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind demanding AI pause
stories.why_it_matters: Protesters gathered outside the San Francisco offices of OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind this week, demanding a pause in AI development over safety concerns. The demonstrations show growing public unease about how fast AI is advancing without adequate safety testing or regulation. While protests alone won't slow development, they add political pressure that could eventually lead to tougher laws — relevant for companies like Alphabet (GOOG) that are at the centre of the AI race.

stories.title: Meta launches Muse Spark 1.1 — enters the developer AI API market
stories.why_it_matters: Meta has launched Muse Spark 1.1, a new AI model aimed at software developers, and entered the API (Application Programming Interface — the system that lets developers plug AI into their own apps) market. This puts Meta in direct competition with OpenAI, Google and Anthropic for developer mindshare. The more companies offer capable AI tools to developers, the faster AI gets embedded into everyday products — and the more competitive pressure lands on Google's existing developer ecosystem.

stories.title: AI regulation is 'answering the wrong question', says Lowy Institute
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's Lowy Institute published a sharp critique today arguing that current AI regulation efforts — both globally and in Australia — are focused on the wrong things. Rather than trying to write rules for specific AI behaviours (which change rapidly), the institute argues regulators should focus on systemic risks and accountability structures. This is an important counterpoint to Canberra's new framework — the debate about *how* to regulate AI, not just whether to, is very much alive.

stories.title: AI in schools: New players enter the race to shape how kids learn with AI
stories.why_it_matters: A new wave of tech companies are entering the AI-in-schools space, competing to shape how children learn with artificial intelligence tools. The competition is heating up beyond just the big names — startups and education-specific platforms are pitching AI tutors, lesson planners and assessment tools to school districts. For parents and investors, this signals AI's rapid move from Silicon Valley labs into everyday classrooms — a multi-billion dollar market that's just getting started.

sport.summary: NRL Round 20 kicks off tomorrow night with Panthers vs Broncos at CommBank Stadium. The Broncos' finals hopes are fading fast. In the AFL, Max Gawn's looming exit from Melbourne is making headlines, and the Jarome Luai rugby switch rumour continues to swirl.

stories.title: Broncos' finals hopes virtually gone as losing streak continues
stories.why_it_matters: The Brisbane Broncos' losing streak has extended to the point where the ABC is reporting their finals hopes are 'virtually an impossible task'. Their Round 20 clash tomorrow night against the Panthers at CommBank Stadium (7:50 PM) is a must-win — but they're taking on one of the competition's top sides. A loss effectively ends their season. Gold Coast fans heading to Cbus Super Stadium on Sunday can catch Titans vs Sea Eagles at 2:00 PM.

stories.title: Jarome Luai rugby union switch: Cameron Cronk floats shock move
stories.why_it_matters: Former NRL player Cameron Cronk has floated the idea of Wests Tigers star Jarome Luai making a shock switch to rugby union. Luai is one of the NRL's most exciting playmakers, and the suggestion has drawn criticism — some calling it a 'band-aid' move for whatever rugby union club might pursue him. Luai is off-contract and his future is one of the hottest topics in the player market heading into the second half of the season.

stories.title: Max Gawn exit from Melbourne Demons 'inevitable' — will leave biggest hole in AFL
stories.why_it_matters: SEN is reporting that Melbourne Demons ruckman Max Gawn's exit from the club is now seen as inevitable, and that his departure will leave 'the biggest hole of any AFL club'. Gawn is widely considered the best ruckman of his generation — losing him would be a massive blow to Melbourne's flag hopes. No official announcement yet, but the speculation is ramping up.

stories.title: AFL team whispers: Young Cat to debut, Swan 'good to go', Tiger to return
stories.why_it_matters: Ahead of this weekend's AFL fixtures, AFL.com.au's team whispers column has a young Geelong Cat set to make their debut, a Sydney Swan confirmed 'good to go' after an injury scare, and a Wests Tigers player returning from a layoff. No specific names confirmed in the available data, but worth checking the full article if your team is in action this weekend.
